name: Sinharaja Forest Reserve
blurb: Sri Lanka's last big lowland rainforest, from giant trees to the leopard.

tip.title: Remove the figs
tip.text: Fruiting trees feed monkeys, pigeons and bulbuls. Lower the wild figs and watch the fruit-eaters, then the leopard that hunts the monkeys.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage: Sinharaja Forest Reserve

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Sinharaja Forest Reserve, Purple-faced langur, Sri Lankan leopard). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.name: Wild figs
nodes.desc: Fig trees fruit through much of the year in tropical forests and are a widely used food for fruit-eating birds and monkeys.
A common flowering shrub of forest clearings and edges. GloBI records show bulbuls eating its fruit.
A well-recorded songbird that eats fruit and insects. GloBI records include it eating Melastoma and being eaten by the green vine snake.
Leaf-eating insects, beetles, crickets and other small invertebrates that feed on leaves and litter and are prey for lizards, frogs and birds.
A large lizard that eats frogs and other small animals, and also scavenges carrion.
The island apex predator, living in forests across Sri Lanka. It hunts monkeys and other mammals, and no larger carnivore competes with it.
Roughly 3,600 to 5,000 mm of rain per year falls in two monsoons, keeping the forest wet all year.

nodes.name: Fungi, termites & litter fauna
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves, wood and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.

story: Sinharaja Forest Reserve is the last virgin rainforest left in Sri Lanka, covering 36,000 hectares. Over 60% of its trees are endemic. It is home to 19 of Sri Lanka's 20 endemic birds.
matters: Total vegetation density is estimated at 240,000 plants per hectare. Endemic species include the green pit viper and the Sri Lankan birdwing butterfly.
